query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Lightweight HEAs that incorporate high fractions of light elements (such as Al and Ti) can achieve low density while retaining high mechanical strength and corrosion/oxidation resistance because the light-element additions generate pronounced lattice distortion. This distortion both enhances solid-solution strengthening (reducing dislocation mobility) and promotes the formation of a homogeneous, adherent, and protective oxide/passive layer at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional or high-density HEA with lower amounts of light elements that typically exhibits less lattice distortion and a less uniform microstructure.
generation.intervention: Design and synthesize an equiatomic or near-equiatomic lightweight HEA alloy with increased concentrations of light elements (e.g., Al, Ti) to induce greater lattice distortion, using controlled processing (e.g., rapid solidification or sputtering) to favor amorphous or nano‐crystalline microstructures.
generation.conditions: The alloy should be tested under high-temperature oxidation (e.g., exposure at ~900 °C) and in corrosive environments (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl solution), as well as subjected to mechanical loading (e.g., tensile or compression tests) to assess strength retention.
generation.structural_mediator: A homogeneous amorphous/nano-crystalline matrix with significant lattice distortion that facilitates the formation of a continuous, protective oxide/passive film.
generation.mechanism: The increased lattice distortion from the light-element additions impedes dislocation motion (thereby enhancing strength) while also encouraging a uniform formation of protective Al2O3, Cr2O3, or mixed oxide scales that improve high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance. This dual effect helps maintain low density without sacrificing performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: When compared to a baseline HEA with fewer light elements, the modified lightweight HEA will exhibit a higher yield strength, lower corrosion current density, reduced mass gain during oxidation exposure, and overall improved durability while maintaining a lower density.
generation.baseline: High-density HEAs or conventional alloys with low light-element content that do not develop as pronounced a lattice distortion or uniform oxide/passivation layers under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: If the alloy composition or processing conditions lead to unwanted phase separation or the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds (i.e., if the increased light-element content goes beyond an optimal range), the expected benefits of lattice distortion and oxide layer formation will be lost, resulting in diminished mechanical and corrosion/oxidation performance.
generation.uncertainty: Although the expected dual role of lattice distortion in strengthening and passive film formation is supported by available observations, the precise quantitative contributions of each mechanism remain uncertain and may depend on specific compositional and process variables.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two HEA samples under identical processing conditions: one with a high content of light elements (e.g., increased Al and Ti levels to promote lattice distortion) and a control alloy with lower light-element levels. Subject both samples to identical high-temperature oxidation (e.g., at 900 °C) and corrosion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl, along with mechanical testing (e.g., tensile and compression tests).
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for phase and microstructure analysis
Mechanical tests (yield strength, ultimate strength, and ductility)
Electrochemical corrosion measurements (corrosion current density, corrosion potential)
Mass gain measurements during high-temperature oxidation to evaluate oxide layer development
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sample with high light-element content does not show statistically significant improvements in yield strength, reduced oxidation mass gain, and lower corrosion current density compared to the control, or if the oxide/passive layer is found to be discontinuous or non-protective, then the proposed hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Lightweight high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of low-density, high strength-to-weight ratio metallic structural material. Understanding their corrosion behavior is crucial for designing microstructures for their practical applications. This work investigates the electrochemical corrosion behavior of lightweight HEAs AlCrTiV0.5Cux (x = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0) in a 0.6 M NaCl solution. These HEAs were produced by vacuum arc melting. In contrast to 304L stainless steel, all of the alloys exhibited lower current density levels caused by self-corrosion, with AlCrTiV0.5 demonstrating the highest corrosion resistance (0.131 μA/cm2). Corrosion resistance decreased along with the content of copper because copper segregation accelerated local corrosion throughout the alloy.

Tseng et al. [] developed a LWHEA containing Be, with a predominant solid solution structure and low level of intermetallic phases, obtained by arc melting. The Al20Be20Fe10Si15Ti35 (atomic percentage composition) alloy delivered unique mechanical properties and oxidation resistance which makes them appropriate for applications in the transportation industry. Sanchez et al. [] studied three lightweight high entropy alloys Al40Cu15Cr15Fe15Si15, Al65Cu5Cr5Si15Mn5Ti5 and Al60Cu10Fe10Cr5Mn5Ni5Mg5 (atomic percentage composition), which were previously designed by CALPHAD modeling. The alloys were produced by large scale vacuum die casting. Even if the cooling rate of the alloys was very low, the number of phases predicted by Thermo-Calc software was larger than those found in the experimental samples. The obtained alloys presented a high hardness to density ratio, due to the presence of complex precipitates in the as-cast structure.

The simultaneous improvement of mechanical and corrosion resistance is of great significance for engineering applications. In this work, a novel lightweight amorphous structure AlTiVNb high-entropy alloy (HEA) film was fabricated by magnetron sputtering. The compression test of the AlTiVNb HEA film nanopillar exhibits a high compressive strength of up to 3.6 GPa and deformability approaching 58%. The high strength is affected by the disordered state, the nanostructure, and the lattice distortion effect, while the high ductility comes from the ductile shear band and the island structure. In addition, the AlTiVNb HEA film shows a current density of 4.90 × 10−8 A/cm2 and a potential of −0.234 V in the 3.5% NaCl solution, comparable to that of the 316L stainless steel. The chemical disorder state, cocktail effect, and homogeneous amorphous structure contribute to excellent corrosion resistance. This finding offers new insights into high-performance HEA films with robust mechanical and anticorrosion performances for microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials.
